Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small sailboat with a red hull and a white triangular sail on calm teal water at sunset, with a low purple hill on the left and the sun setting just above the horizon.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

10 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The sailboat and its reflection, right of center (hull 68-86% across, 57-63% down), with the sun at 48% across, 42% down as a second accent. Light: Backlight from the setting sun, low in the center of the sky (48% across, 42% down), just above the horizon. Lit edges face the sun: the left and top edges of the sail and hull get the brightest touches, and the sun lays a golden path straight down the water below it.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: laying and blending the sky bandsFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: outlining and filling the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: the hill and the shoreline bandFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: the horizontal dashesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the mast and the boomLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #4 round: the cream line along the top of the hullRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8Step 9Step 10

STEP 1 OF 10

Paint the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the setting sun, low in the middle (48% across, 42% down). Every highlight in this painting faces it.
  2. Twilight lavender, creamy, in long side-to-side strokes across the top 9%, edge to edge.
  3. Below it add bands while wet: Sunset pink to 18% down, Coral glow to 27%, then Sunset orange down to about 60%, well past where the water starts. Blend each join with a few side-to-side strokes.
  4. Work Peach glow into the orange around 48% across, 42% down, a soft patch about 20% wide.
  5. Done: the top 60% is sky in soft bands; the bottom 40% is still white canvas.

  • Sunset pink new3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine
  • Coral glow new3 parts red, 3 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna
  • Sunset orange new3 parts red, 2 parts yellow, 2 parts white
  • Peach glow new3 parts yellow, 3 parts white, 2 parts red

Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge before a big area.

Mix plenty of Sunset orange; it covers the biggest area and comes back for the sun path.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat side to side across the whole canvas, then stroke back over each join while it's wet so the bands melt together.

Watch out: Stopping the sky at the horizon. Run the orange down to about 60%; the hill and water cover the edge later.

Watch out: Blending until it turns muddy. Stop as soon as the paint drags.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 10

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. Sun yellow, creamy: outline a circle centered 48% across, 42.5% down, about 5% of the canvas wide (from 45.5% to 51% across).
  3. Fill it with small circular strokes.
  4. Once dry, give it a second coat so no orange shows through.

Brushes

#6 round

Strokes

Small circles with the brush tip. Turn the round in small circles inside the outline so the sun fills evenly with a soft edge.

Watch out: A lopsided sun. Trace lightly around a bottle cap first if it helps.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 10

Paint the far hill and shoreline

  1. Let the sky dry. Hill purple, creamy: outline the hill from the left edge at 44% down to a peak at 13% across, 40% down, then down to 47% across, 50% down.
  2. Fill it with horizontal strokes. Pull a little Shore indigo into the left end, away from the sun.
  3. Shore indigo: a level band across the whole width, 50% to 54% down.
  4. Flat almost dry, a little Coral glow: skim streaks down the right slope, which faces the sun, and a thin haze above the shoreline's right half.
  5. Done: orange shows below the shoreline, then white canvas.

Brushes

3/4 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes for distant land. Keep the flat level and the strokes long so the far hill and shore stay soft and flat.

Dry brush. Wipe the flat nearly clean and skim lightly down the slope so the coral catches in broken streaks.

Watch out: A tilted horizon. Check the shoreline against the canvas edge or a ruler.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 10

Lay in the teal water

  1. Light teal, creamy, in long side-to-side strokes starting right under the shoreline at 54% down.
  2. Work down to the bottom edge, adding more Deep teal as you go, so the bottom third is the deepest.
  3. Blend the joins with long level strokes while wet, leaving a few streaks of both.
  4. Done: no white canvas anywhere. Keep the water plain teal; the faint warm patches in the picture are not paint to copy.

This is the ugly stage: it looks plain and unfinished, and that's normal. The sun path and boat bring it to life.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes for water. Long level strokes edge to edge; lighter and smoother near the horizon, deeper toward the bottom.

Watch out: Tilted strokes. Keep every stroke level so the water lies flat.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 10

Dash in the sun path

  1. Let the water dry. Try a few dashes on scrap paper. Sunset orange, light load, edge of the flat: short level dashes straight under the sun, from 54% to 95% down.
  2. Near the horizon keep them short and close (37% to 60% across); lower down make them longer and wider apart.
  3. Add a few stray orange dashes on the left water, out to 7% across, around 72% and 80% down.
  4. Peach glow dashes in the middle of the column, then a few Sun yellow dashes just under the sun, each covering less than the last.
  5. Done: teal shows between every dash.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal dashes on water. Touch the chisel edge down and slide it sideways a short way; small and close near the horizon, longer and farther apart in front.

Watch out: A solid stripe. Leave teal gaps between the dashes.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 10

Paint the sail

  1. Let everything dry.
  2. Mark dots as in the diagram: the top at 81% across, 27% down; base corners at 73% and 90% across, 57% down; and 81% across, 57% down.
  3. Sail white, creamy: fill the left triangle, then the right one against the shared tall edge, pulling strokes down from the top.
  4. Give it 2 to 3 thin coats, drying between. On the last, while wet, pull 3 or 4 thin streaks of Sail white plus a touch of Light teal down the right half.

Building from pieces. Paint the left triangle first, then the right one against its tall edge.

Watch out: One thick coat of white. It goes streaky and pink; thin coats cover better.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 10

Paint the red hull

  1. Let the sail dry.
  2. Build the hull as in the diagram: first a long flat strip from 72% to 93% across, its top edge at 58% down.
  3. Then a curved underside down to 63% that tips up to a point at the left (the bow). The right end is square.
  4. Boat red, creamy: fill it with strokes along the hull.
  5. While wet, pull a little Reflection red along the bottom edge for the shadow.

STEP 8 OF 10

Add the mast and the lit edges

  1. Let the boat dry. Try a liner line on scrap paper.
  2. Mast brown thinned to ink, liner: one straight stroke up the sail's shared edge at 81% across, from 26% to 59% down.
  3. Then the boom: a short line from 81% to 90% across at 57.5% down.
  4. Sail white, creamy, #4 round: one solid thin line along the top of the hull from the bow to the stern, closing the gap under the sail.

STEP 9 OF 10

Pull down the boat's reflection

  1. Let everything above the water dry.
  2. Reflection red, flat wiped nearly dry: short downward strokes under the hull, 72% to 92% across, 63% to 69% down.
  3. While wet, drag the wiped flat with Light teal sideways through it in 3 or 4 places, so it breaks into ragged rows.
  4. Same with Sail white under the sail, 69% to 90% down, rows narrowing going down; add Light teal to every third row.
  5. Let it dry. Mast brown, thinned, small round: a zigzag line down from the mast at 81% across to 95% down.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat#4 round

Strokes

Vertical pull-down. Wipe the flat nearly dry and stroke straight down from the waterline, light pressure, so the strokes stay streaky.

Horizontal dashes on water. Drag the wiped flat sideways through the wet reflection so it breaks into rows with ragged ends.

Zigzag. Wiggle the round side to side as you pull down, so the mast line bends like it does on moving water.

Watch out: A reflection as sharp as the boat. Keep it broken and a little darker than the sail.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 10 OF 10

Add ripples and sparkles

  1. Let the water dry. Sunset orange, then Peach glow: short dashes along the shoreline from 27% to 65% across, so the glow spreads wide.
  2. Sun yellow: a second, smaller layer of dashes in the middle of the sun path.
  3. Light teal, edge of the flat: about eight short level ripple dashes on the open water, not in the sun path. A few Deep teal dashes along the left of the sail's reflection.
  4. Titanium white, liner: three to five tiny sparkles beside the brightest part of the sun path.
  5. Yours will look a little different, and that's fine.

Numbers are steps. A dashed, struck-through number was tried on that rung first and didn't hold up. Claude starts at the top and pays for a render only when nothing free will do.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red-hulled sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset, a purple hill on the left, the sun just above the horizon.

Found in the image: Just the picture: no bars, buttons, borders, captions, watermark, or surrounding scene.

Done: Nothing cropped.

Why: Everything in the image is part of the scene to paint.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (11x14 turned to follow the wide picture)

Done: crop

Left out: about 7.5% from each side (15% in all): a strip of open water and sky on the right past the boat and the left end of the hill.

Why: The picture is 3:2 and the canvas 14:11, so a crop keeps everything that matters for free: the boat and its reflection, the sun and its path, and the hill's slope stay whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: tiny_separate_things: No. The only small separate thing is the sailboat, and it is the subject.; textures_of_hundreds: No. The water ripples and sky streaks are one repeated mark each (horizontal strokes and dashes).; detail_inside_big_shapes: No. Sky, hill, and water are smooth gradients and flat shapes; the sun path is a column of horizontal dashes.; more_parts_than_budget: No. About 7 parts (sky, sun, far hill and shoreline, water, sun path, boat, boat reflection) against max_parts 8 (11x14 is 154 sq in, budget as is).

Changed: none

Why: Every answer was no, so the lesson is made from the photo itself.

Already a simple painting: a sunset sky in soft bands, a far purple hill, teal water, and one red-and-white sailboat with its reflection. What matters is a smooth sky gradient, a level horizon, the boat's crisp triangle-on-strip silhouette, and water that reads as water (horizontal dashes for the sun path, broken rows for the reflection). The hard parts for a beginner are white over orange (several coats) and keeping the reflection softer than the boat. The lesson is about painting back to front and the water-reflection order.

Subject: A small sailboat with a red hull and a white triangular sail on calm teal water at sunset, with a low purple hill on the left and the sun setting just above the horizon.
Focal point: The sailboat and its reflection, right of center (hull 68-86% across, 57-63% down), with the sun at 48% across, 42% down as a second accent.
Light: Backlight from the setting sun, low in the center of the sky (48% across, 42% down), just above the horizon. Lit edges face the sun: the left and top edges of the sail and hull get the brightest touches, and the sun lays a golden path straight down the water below it.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sunset sky gradient: lavender purple at the top, pink, coral, then orange down to the horizon, lightest around the sun
  2. the sun: a pale yellow disk
  3. far purple hill on the left and the low dark shoreline along the horizon
  4. teal water, lighter near the horizon and deeper at the bottom, in horizontal strokes
  5. golden sun path of horizontal dashes under the sun
  6. white sail (two triangles)
  7. red hull
  8. mast, boom, and the lit edges of the boat
  9. the boat's reflection: red under the hull, broken white under the sail, a zigzag mast line
  10. light ripple dashes across the water and sparkles on the sun path
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A simple sunset seascape (sky gradient, far hill, water, one sailboat) painted back to front on white canvas is exactly the paint-along, YouTube-style beginner lesson; the technique also has water-reflection rules and stroke results for sun paths, pull-downs, zigzags, and ripples this photo needs.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

Starts from a toned ground and a sketch with a fixed stage list (tone, sketch, background, block-in, build-up, details); the owner's default for acrylic beginners is paint-along, and the fixed stages would give no steps for the sun path and reflections.

How the paint recipes were worked out15 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order10 steps

Back to front, as the technique and research ask: the sky first, run down past the horizon; the sun on the dry sky; the far hill and shoreline over the sky; the water over the sky's lower edge; then the sun path on the water, then the boat above the water (sail, hull, mast and lit rim), then the boat's reflection once the boat is dry, and ripple dashes and sparkles last over dry water, in the research's reflection order.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky

    The farthest thing and the biggest area; it runs past the horizon so later layers cover its edge.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Sits on the sky and behind everything else; it goes on once the sky is dry so the yellow stays clean.

  3. 3. Paint the far hill and shoreline

    The farthest land, painted over the dry sky; the shoreline sets the horizon every later step keeps.

  4. 4. Lay in the teal water

    The water covers the rest of the canvas before anything sits on it.

  5. 5. Dash in the sun path

    The sun's reflection belongs to the water and lies behind the boat, so it goes on before the boat.

  6. 6. Paint the sail

    The sail is the boat's biggest piece and goes on first so the hull can overlap its base.

  7. 7. Paint the red hull

    The hull sits in front of the sail's lower edge and on the water.

  8. 8. Add the mast and the lit edges

    Thin dark lines and the cream rim need the sail and hull dry underneath (liner work over dry paint).

  9. 9. Pull down the boat's reflection

    Reflections go on after everything above the water is dry, straight under the boat.

  10. 10. Add ripples and sparkles

    Ripple dashes and sparkles go on dry water last, with the second, smaller sun-path layer after a dry wait.

Filters it tried11 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

The sky, sun, hill, water, sun path, and final ripples are fills, gradients, or one repeated mark that words and picture cover. The boat arrives in three steps as new shapes (sail, hull, reflection), and each got a diagram; the mast step is two straight lines given by position.

  • Step 6: Paint the sail beginner check

    Noticed: A tall, narrow shape appears whole in one step, and the text review found 'as in the diagram' with no diagram.

    Pieces: Four placement dots, the left triangle, the right one against the shared tall edge (where the mast goes later), then cool streaks on the last coat.

  • Step 7: Paint the red hull beginner check

    Noticed: The bow's upward point and the curved underside are hard to picture from numbers.

    Pieces: A long flat strip, then the curved underside tipping up to the bow, then the dark line along the bottom.

  • Step 9: Pull down the boat's reflection beginner check

    Noticed: The order of moves (pull down, drag sideways, rows, zigzag) needs more than a sentence.

    Pieces: Red pulled down under the hull, teal dragged sideways through it, cream and pale blue rows narrowing downward, then the zigzag mast line once dry.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A gradient in horizontal bands; the words give each band's position.
  • Step 2: A circle with a center and width given.
  • Step 3: A simple mound and a level band, with the peak and ends given as positions.
  • Step 4: A flat gradient in level strokes.
  • Step 5: One repeated mark (level dashes) with where they go and how they change down the canvas.
  • Step 8: Two straight lines and one rim line, each placed by position.
  • Step 10: A count of one repeated mark and a few sparkles, placed in words.

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

Rerendered once from the first finish and the photo with a smooth lavender, pink, orange gradient; the second render matches the photo.

  • Round 1 Step 7: The stray orange sun-path dashes on the left of the water were missing. (fixed by lock-steps: outside the step's region, put back from the step before)
  • Round 1 Step 8: The sun path turned into a soft blurred glow column; its separate dashes and the stray left dashes were gone. (fixed by lock-steps: the sun path is outside this step's region, so the lock put back the previous step's dashes)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The first sky render stopped at the horizon although the plan said 62%; a redo with an explicit fix worked.
  • lock-steps' backward pass tinted the plain water step with warm ghost bands where the finish has the sun path; the raw render was clean. Recorded as a known problem rather than skipping the lock.
  • With a backlit scene it's easy to put the shadow on the wrong side: the text review caught Shore indigo on the hill slope that faces the sun.
  • The research teaches reflections as vertical pull-downs crossed by horizontal dashes; the rendered reflection was ragged horizontal rows, so the text has the painter drag teal sideways through the wet pull-down. Doing that wet is my own adaptation, not from the research.
  • The cool Light teal streaks on the sail are my reading of the finish, not from the research.

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.
